name: Sicilian: Maróczy Bind
summary: The Maróczy Bind (pawns on c4 and e4) clamps the d5 and b5 squares, giving White space and a slow squeeze against the Sicilian.
intro: The Maróczy Bind arises after 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4, when White plants pawns on c4 and e4. This broad duo controls the key d5 and b5 squares, denying Black the freeing breaks ...d5 and ...b5 that normally power Sicilian counterplay. It is most often seen against the Accelerated Dragon and leads to a strategic battle between White's space and Black's compact, resilient setup.
line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 c4 Nf6 Nc3 d6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The defining feature of the position is White's pawn duo on c4 and e4. This bind exerts a firm grip on d5, the very square Black most wants to occupy or trade into, and it also discourages the queenside expansion ...b5. In return for surrendering this space, Black obtains a solid, flexible structure with no weaknesses and a well-placed fianchettoed bishop on g7 that eyes the long dark diagonal. The strategic contest revolves around whether White can convert the extra space into a lasting initiative before Black completes development and generates counterplay.

Black's standard method is to exchange a pair of knights with ...Nxd4, easing the cramp, and to reroute the remaining knight via ...Nd7-c5 to pressure e4 and the queenside. Play often centres on the c-file, where Black stacks rooks against the c4-pawn, and on the d4 and d5 squares. White, meanwhile, aims to keep the bind intact, complete development with Be2, O-O, Be3 and often Rc1 or Qd2, and expand slowly. A recurring theme is Black's thematic ...b5 pawn sacrifice, offering a pawn to break the bind and activate the pieces, forcing White to decide between accepting and defending or declining to preserve the clamp.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: Against the Accelerated Dragon the main tabiya arises after 5...Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 O-O 8.Be2, when Black most often chooses the classical Gurgenidze plan with ...Nxd4 and ...Be6, pressuring c4 and preparing ...Qa5 and rook play on the c-file. An important alternative is 7...Ng4, hitting the e3-bishop and forcing concessions before Black settles the structure. The move order given here, with ...Nf6 and ...d6, reaches the same family of Maróczy structures that also occur by transposition from the Hedgehog and the English Opening.

The Gurgenidze system, named after Bukhuti Gurgenidze, remains the principal method for Black, aiming for the ...b5 break or piece pressure against the c4- and e4-pawns. Alternatively Black may adopt a more restrained, Hedgehog-like setup with ...d6, ...a6, ...b6 and ...e6, coiling behind the third rank and waiting to strike with ...b5 or ...d5 at the right moment. White's most testing setups keep the pieces on natural squares and answer Black's activity by exchanging active minor pieces or by advancing the f-pawn to gain kingside space and tighten the grip.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The bind is named after Géza Maróczy (1870–1951), the leading Hungarian grandmaster of the early twentieth century, who demonstrated the strength of the c4 and e4 pawn formation against the Sicilian and other openings. For decades the structure discouraged players from the Accelerated Dragon, since the early ...g6 allowed White to erect the clamp with c4. Interest revived in the second half of the twentieth century, when Gurgenidze and later a generation of dynamic defenders showed that Black's position, though cramped, was resourceful and hard to break down. Today the Maróczy Bind is regarded as a critical positional test rather than a refutation, appearing across the Accelerated Dragon, the Kan and Taimanov Sicilians, and by transposition from the English Opening.
